accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS 3.OA.D.9 (identify arithmetic patterns in the multiplication table and explain them using properties of operations; its own example is that 4 times a number is always even) and the NC England Year 3–4 multiplication statements (recall to 12 × 12 by Year 4; use commutativity and known facts). Every value recomputed: SORT products 15, 28, 54, 49, 24, 45 and their parities; fold pairs 3×8/8×3 = 24 (other 24 is 4×6), 2×9/9×2 = 18 (other 18 is 3×6), 4×6/6×4, 7×5/5×7 = 35; rows 3+3 = 6 (×7: 21+21 = 42), 3+4 = 7 (×4: 12+16 = 28), 4+5 = 9 (×6: 24+30 = 54); 9s 36, 45, 54, 63, 72, 81 with digit sums 9 and distractors 9k+1 and 10k; claims about the 3s (3 × 2 = 6 breaks it), 4s, 5s, 10s and odd × odd. The digit-sum rule is stated only up to 9 × 10, where it holds (9 × 11 = 99 does not). Parameterised answers 6n, 9n, 10n and 8n are whole numbers at n = 2, 6 and 10.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented errors in times-table reasoning (NCETM ready-to-progress 3NF-1/4NF-1 on using known facts and commutativity; Askew et al. on derived facts): judging parity from one factor (7 × 6 called odd: prediction, sort feedback, practice p1, challenge oddodd/depends), treating a fact and its turnaround as separate facts (fold step, m8, challenge neigh/swapone), multiplying or mis-adding row numbers instead of adding lots (row feedback names the row actually made; challenge addrow/multrow; m2 offers row 12), in the 9s using 10 × n or a number whose digits do not add to 9 (each distractor generated from that pattern; challenge digsum/tenk/plusten), and accepting a claim from a few cases (claims step, p5 with the 3, 9, 15 trap).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagttpat is built on the 10 × 10 multiplication square itself: parity colouring that fills in as facts are sorted, a dashed fold line on the leading diagonal with mirror-cell tapping, row-header picking that adds two rows into a third, a hidden 9s row with digit-pattern distractors, and claim testing with highlighted rows. It differs from flagtt12 (12 × 12 facts), flagttdbl and flagttfam (deriving one table from another), flagcommul (arrays for commutativity) and flagoddn (odd and even numbers); the lab_distinct gate passes under 30% shingle overlap with every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each pattern before the text states it: the orange odd cells appear only where both factors are odd as the sort proceeds, and when the task ends the whole square is coloured so the checkerboard of odd rows and columns is visible; tapping a same-answer cell such as 4 × 6 for the mirror of 3 × 8 is refused with the reason, so the swap-row-and-column rule is found by doing; building row 7 from rows 3 and 4 shows the sum of the two answers next to 7 × 4; filling the 9s one by one shows the tens rising and ones falling. Each step's summary appears only when its task is complete.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: whether 7 × 6 is even or odd (Odd tempts because 7 is odd; the colouring shows one even factor makes it even), what folding the square on its diagonal does (Nothing matches tempts; the mirror pairs light up), and which number is in the 9 times table (56 tempts as a familiar product, 64 as a near-miss; the digit-sum pattern shows 63). A.reveal echoes the locked-in choice when the task completes.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with two wrong options each and nine distinct messages (oddodd, depends, neigh, swapone, addrow, multrow, digsum, tenk, other, plusten), e.g. multrow: 'Rows add, they do not multiply. 3 lots + 4 lots = 7 lots, so row 4.' In-lab misses also name the slip with numbers, e.g. 'Row 2 + row 3 makes row 5, not row 6: 2 × 7 + 3 × 7 = 35, but 6 × 7 = 42.' and 'That 24 is 4 × 6, a different fact with the same answer.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons.py passes the learner limits; kid paragraphs read at about FK grade 0–3 (overall about 1) and the adult text at about grade 8. Kid sentences are short and concrete ('Rows add up. 2 sevens and 4 sevens make 6 sevens.'), and the precise words are used and explained: factor, product (answer), even, odd, row, column, diagonal, times table, turnaround; the adult text names commutative and distributive properties.

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches and explanation overlap with every other lesson is under 12%. Each lab step has one job (parity, symmetry, adding rows, the 9s, testing claims), and every feedback line carries a fact or a counterexample. Item explanations give the reason (4 × n = 2 × (2 × n); 9 × n = 10 × n − n) rather than restating the answer.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px in light and dark on every step, before and after Show me. First-pass fixes: the footer message covered the 9s option boxes and the True/False boxes on phones (the panel now reserves room for a three-line message and the canvas is taller on narrow screens), and the even/odd step showed the product next to the boxes and kept the gold ring on the previous fact (it now asks whether either factor is even and the ring moves to the current fact). Grid cells are about 30 px at 360 px wide and every cell action also has a full-size button below the canvas; the canvas keeps a light card in dark mode.

accessibility.evidence: Everything is doable with buttons: Even and Odd, one button per candidate mirror cell ('8 × 3', '4 × 6', '3 × 9'), Row 1 to Row n−1 for building rows, one button per 9s option and True/False for claims, each with an aria-label naming the action. The canvas aria-label reports the current fact, options and progress after every action ('Find the mirror of 3 × 8 across the diagonal. Options: 8 × 3, 4 × 6, 3 × 9.'), and challenge feedback is an aria-live status. walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors.
